metadata.title: Teacher job satisfaction: International evidence on the role of school working conditions and teacher characteristics

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TIMSS 2019 eighth-grade mathematics teacher questionnaire data across 46 education systems. Although TIMSS employs a two-stage cluster stratified sampling design (schools sampled with PPS, then intact classes), the authors explicitly state they did not use teacher weights because the analysis is teacher-level and focuses on teacher-related predictors rather than student-level outcomes. As a result, complex survey weighting is not incorporated into the regression estimates, which may leave some clustering-related variance under-accounted. The analytic sample is restricted to teachers with complete data across the latent constructs and predictors, implemented via listwise deletion.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This study’s dependent variable is teacher job satisfaction measured directly from TIMSS 2019 teacher questionnaire items (a Likert-type affective scale), not a cognitive achievement score generated via plausible values. Because the outcome is non-PV and the analysis is based on latent-variable scales and regression on those scale scores, plausible-value handling is not applicable. Missing data handling is reported as listwise deletion due to low item-level missingness (~10%).

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Secondary analysis of TIMSS 2019 teacher questionnaire data restricted to eighth-grade mathematics teachers. The authors treat each teacher response as an independent observation (no school/classroom-level variables included). They apply listwise deletion because item-level missingness is low (~10%) and they retain only cases with complete data across the latent constructs (teacher job satisfaction, teacher workload, student discipline) and the teacher characteristics (gender, teaching years, mathematics background, professional development).

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 Mathematics (Teacher questionnaire; 46 education systems)
main_findings.target_variable: Teacher job satisfaction (latent scale from 5 items)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Not reported (regression coefficients and significance levels reported; no ML accuracy/AUC/RMSE). Pooled standardized regression estimates: Leadership Support 0.266***; Student Discipline 0.356***; Teacher workload −0.113***; Gender 0.071**; Teaching years −0.006***; Mathematics 0.023 (ns); Mathematics Education −0.029 (ns); PD 0.084***.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 Mathematics teacher questionnaire the study leveraged leadership support, student discipline, teacher workload, professional development hours, and teacher gender to model teacher job satisfaction, finding that leadership support, student discipline, and professional development were positively associated with job satisfaction while teacher workload and teaching years were negatively associated. This indicates that improving school leadership practices, classroom disciplinary climate, and reducing perceived workload—along with investing in professional development—may be effective levers for strengthening teacher well-being and retention, though the study is cross-sectional and does not establish causal effects.

data.outcome_summary: This study uses TIMSS 2019 eighth-grade mathematics teacher questionnaire data from 13,048 teachers across 46 education systems to examine how school working conditions and teacher characteristics relate to teacher job satisfaction. Teacher job satisfaction is measured as an affective latent scale from five Likert-type items, with Cronbach’s alpha of 0.907 for pooled data. The authors first validate the measurement models via CFA and test measurement invariance across countries (metric invariance achieved; scalar invariance not reached, so mean comparisons are limited). In pooled regression models, leadership support (β=0.266***), student discipline (β=0.356***), and professional development (β=0.084***) are positively associated with job satisfaction, while teacher workload (β=−0.113***), teaching years (β=−0.006***), and gender show smaller effects (gender β=0.071**). The analysis uses listwise deletion for ~10% item missingness and explicitly does not apply teacher weights; coefficients are reported rather than ML performance metrics, and the cross-sectional design limits causal interpretation.
